effective_bit_depth — 2D features op

• Data kinds: image → feature

• Call: fullseye.apply(img, "effective_bit_depth", a=0.5, b=0.5) (the 2-D model is one image plus two scalar knobs a,b∈[0,1])

*The figure is the actual output on a synthetic 128×128 input. Left: input, right: output. Point clouds are drawn as a top-down scatter (brightness = z), 1-D series as a line plot, volumes as the maximum-intensity projection along z, videos as the middle frame, complex images as magnitude; return values that are not pictures are shown as the values themselves.*

*Knob a does not change the output (measured: identical at 0.1 / 0.5 / 0.9).*

*Knob b does not change the output (measured: identical at 0.1 / 0.5 / 0.9).*

Usage

Estimates the number of bits the image actually uses and returns it mapped to [0,1] (feature).

Even when stored in an 8-bit container, it is common for the content to be worth only 6 bits — a low-bit sensor that was stretched, a pass through JPEG, a gamma applied, and so on. Here the effective bit count is estimated from the actual spacing of the occupied grey levels:

the pixel values that occur are sorted, the mode of the differences between adjacent values is taken as the step Δ, and bits = log2(1 + 1/Δ). The return value is bits / 16 (a/b are unused).

Conditions of use and how it goes wrong: (1) ★The pixel count sets the upper limit. When the grey levels are almost continuous (images processed in floating point), the smallest step is "the mean spacing ~1/N when there are N values", so the estimate levels off near log2(N) — on a 128x128 (N=16384) continuous image the measurement was 13.7 bit. It does not saturate at 16, so draw the "cannot measure beyond this" line from the pixel count beforehand (measuring on a small crop gives low values). (2) After a nonlinear transform (gamma, logarithm), the step differs by location, so the mode is "a representative step", not a uniform step.

(3) On a dithered image the grey levels get filled in, so the effective bit count comes out high —

that answers "how many levels are used", not "how many bits of information there are".
